title: Japan's Asian Games Face Problems with Athlete Housing
paragraphs: The 2026 Asian Games, held in Japan's Aichi Prefecture and its capital Nagoya from September 19 to October 4, faced serious problems with housing for athletes.

Unlike most major international sporting events, the Games did not have an athletes' village, where competitors usually stay together. In October 2023, the organizing committee decided not to build one in order to control costs. Officials also pointed out that the Games were spread across two prefectures.

Instead, participants were placed in a mix of accommodation. About 4,000 people stayed on a cruise ship, the Costa Serena, which was docked at the port of Nagoya. Another 2,000 stayed in wooden huts, and the rest stayed in hotels across the city and the prefecture.

The problems grew because more people registered for the Games than expected. Organizers had planned for about 15,000 athletes and officials, but the number rose as new sports were added to the program. In total, more than 17,000 people registered.
Organizers even discussed ways of reducing the number of participants after registrations rose far above what they had expected.

Some teams were unhappy with the arrangements. Officials from South Korea described the accommodation as the "worst ever," complaining about a serious shortage of rooms and beds that were too short for athletes. According to reports, some coaches had to be moved to other hotels or to private rentals.
However, not everyone had problems. According to reports, athletes in some sports said they were satisfied with their hotel rooms in Nagoya.

Organizers and the Olympic Council of Asia insisted that everyone who registered before the deadline in July had received suitable accommodation. Tayyab Ikram, an official of the Olympic Council of Asia, pointed out that an athletes' village is not a required part of any Games.
